purpose: Every defect this repository has ever found -- in its tools, in its examples, or in its own documentation -- gets one record. The record is closed only when it answers four questions mechanically: (1) what shape was the defect (class), (2) why did our checking miss it (escape_cause), (3) what root cause was changed, (4) what gate now kills this class and how that gate was shown to fire. A defect recorded as prose cannot be interrogated; a defect recorded here can be, by tools/defect-closure.py.

escape_cause_taxonomy.E1: no gate existed at the time the defect was made
escape_cause_taxonomy.E2: a gate existed but did not cover this shape (substring for structure, first column for the table, a sample set that never contained the case)
escape_cause_taxonomy.E3: a gate fired but had no landing -- printed, noted, logged, and never entered the exit code
escape_cause_taxonomy.E4: a gate existed but had never been shown capable of failing -- a decorative gate; it was believed to be running and it was not discriminating

class_taxonomy: docs/taxonomy.md -- SF-001 .. SF-014 across five families (A Vacuous Verification, B Uncounted Absence, C Wrong Evidence, D Drifting Oracle, E Process & Environment)

entries.symptom: A handler that correctly recorded a failure was reported as a silent one: _silent_body_kinds() accumulated silent statement kinds and returned them if non-empty, never verifying that EVERY statement was silent.
entries.found_by: running the linter on its own source (building-this-catalog #1)
entries.root_cause: the rule tested a property of SOME statements while claiming a property of ALL of them; the sample pair only ever contained all-silent bodies, so the quantifier was never exercised
entries.gate_added: gate-lint.py sample pair extended to a mixed body; the rule returns [] as soon as any statement is not a discard
entries.evidence: the mixed 'record then continue' handler is no longer flagged -- the finding that produced this entry is gone

entries.symptom: SFL-005 decided whether a test runner's output was guarded by searching the raw text for the word 'collected'; the bad sample's docstring contained that word, so the rule concluded a guard existed and stayed silent.
entries.found_by: --selftest: the bad sample was not flagged (building-this-catalog #2)
entries.root_cause: identifier (a guard construct) was detected by substring instead of by structure; the sample's surrounding prose leaked into the detection
entries.gate_added: SFL-005 detects a guard construct via the AST (Compare over a string literal, or a pattern-match call), not a mention in prose
entries.evidence: the bad sample is now flagged by --selftest

entries.symptom: check-catalog.py asserted each entry id appeared in the index files with 'if eid in text'; after a link was deliberately mangled to SF-014-REMOVED the assertion still passed, because 'SF-014' occurs inside the mangled string.
entries.found_by: reverse control A: mangle a link, assert a non-zero exit (building-this-catalog #3)
entries.root_cause: the validator had no negative control that mangled a link, so it had never been observed failing on the exact shape it existed to catch
entries.gate_added: check-catalog.py asserts the entry FILENAME is linked, not that its id occurs as text; reverse control A is part of the suite
entries.evidence: mangling a link now forces a non-zero exit

entries.symptom: gate-lint.py /nonexistent/path.py printed 'no Python files found' and exited 0 -- being asked to check something that does not exist and reporting success.
entries.found_by: reverse control B (building-this-catalog #4)
entries.root_cause: an empty target set was treated as a pass; the gate had never been run against a target that does not exist
entries.gate_added: explicit targets that do not exist are a failure; so is 'nothing was linted'
entries.evidence: gate-lint on a missing path now exits non-zero

entries.symptom: Tree-level findings (SFL-006) were printed but never added to the severity counters; the visible output contained a finding while --strict exited 0.
entries.found_by: reverse control C run in strict mode (building-this-catalog #5)
entries.root_cause: the finding had no landing: it was reported into a channel that did not feed the exit code, and nothing required a reported finding to move it
entries.gate_added: tree-level findings enter the same counters as file-level ones; reverse control C
entries.evidence: --strict with a tree-level finding now exits non-zero

entries.symptom: '# gate-lint: ignore SFL-001' was matched with a plain regex over the source; gate-lint.py's own docstring quotes that directive, so the file suppressed SFL-001 for itself.
entries.found_by: reading the inline-suppressions note in the linter's own output (building-this-catalog #6)
entries.root_cause: the suppression directive was matched anywhere in the text rather than only inside a comment token
entries.gate_added: the directive is honoured only inside a tokenize.COMMENT token; if the source cannot be tokenised, suppressions are ignored (fail toward 'checked')
entries.evidence: gate-lint.py no longer suppresses SFL-001 for itself

entries.symptom: Unreadable files were announced on stdout and then dropped; the run could still exit 0. An unlinted file is an unverified file.
entries.found_by: reading the SFL-002 finding on the linter's own source (building-this-catalog #7)
entries.root_cause: the problem had a representation (a printed line) but no landing: no path carried it into the exit code, so an unlinted file looked like a clean run
entries.gate_added: unreadable files are counted, listed, and force a non-zero exit
entries.evidence: an unreadable input now forces a non-zero exit

entries.symptom: SFL-003 was released at severity 'medium'; measured against two files of ordinary tooling it produced four findings and zero true positives, while still affecting the exit code.
entries.found_by: running the linter on its own source and reading every finding (building-this-catalog #8)
entries.root_cause: a rule's stated confidence was not the measured one; nothing required a rule to be run against ordinary code and its precision read before release
entries.gate_added: sample-pair requirement + a rule must declare its MEASURED confidence and known false positives; SFL-003 demoted to low/confidence-low, scoped to module level
entries.evidence: SFL-003 now carries its measured precision in its own false-positives note

entries.symptom: make-manifest.py rebound 'digest' inside a loop and returned the hash of the last file instead of the set digest; the file written to disk was correct, the printed/returned value was wrong, and the tool's own verifier then rejected the tool's own output.
entries.found_by: --check disagreeing with the generator's own stdout (building-this-catalog #9)
entries.root_cause: no gate required a reported value to be produced by a second, independent route; one expression both wrote the artifact and supplied the return value
entries.gate_added: generate / --check / --print-digest must all yield one identical value (three independent channels)
entries.evidence: the three channels agree after the loop variable was renamed to file_digest

entries.symptom: A comment claimed the '(?:\.git)?' token was load-bearing and that selftest case 3 had caught a false positive from its absence; re-running case 3 against the 'broken' regex showed it passes under both, so the claim described a defect that never existed.
entries.found_by: testing a comment instead of trusting it (building-this-catalog #10)
entries.root_cause: the claim was produced by reasoning, not by running; selftest case 3 could not distinguish the two regexes, so the suite had no power over the claim
entries.gate_added: AGENTS rule 10 (do not assert a necessity you have not measured) + the claim was replaced by the measured result, with the measurement kept
entries.evidence: case 3 passes under both regexes -- the original claim is now recorded as measured-false

entries.symptom: Five statements across three files claimed CI ran the gates and enforced the manifest; .github/workflows/ did not exist. The repository whose subject is 'a check believed to be running, and not running' had a CI believed to be running and not running.
entries.found_by: writing .github/workflows/gates.yml and pushing it (building-this-catalog #11)
entries.root_cause: no gate existed that checked whether a workflow the documentation asserted actually exists; an absent run emits nothing and looked identical to a run that passed
entries.gate_added: .github/workflows/gates.yml added and the README badge repointed at the real run
entries.evidence: the workflow's first execution failed a gate that a local run had reported passing

entries.symptom: check_readme_agreement() compared only the FIRST column of the S5 crosswalk table; a change in the semantic mapping columns (the exact Q4/D1 drift the previous correction was about) stayed green.
entries.found_by: ITU FG-TIDA round-3 review (use-cases#21, comment 6033701828, 2026-10-07T08:04Z), confirmed by our own gate 9 on first run
entries.root_cause: the mutation suite M1-M4 all targeted the artifact under test (implementation.py); not one mutation was aimed at a checker, so the gate's own blind spot (first column standing in for the whole table) was never exercised by anything we ran
entries.gate_added: gate 9 (tools/checker-mutation.py) + _readme_agreement_negative_controls(); the agreement gate now compares every normalised column
entries.evidence: tampering crosswalk column 2 or column 3 now turns the selftest red; restoring returns it to green

entries.symptom: The act-window branch still pre-classified the temporal answer: it injected freeze_state = FREEZE_POST_VERDICT directly, and the binding-token structure changed with it, so Q6's own inference ('the binding was lost when the freeze landed after the verdict') was handed to it rather than derived.
entries.found_by: ITU FG-TIDA round-3 review (use-cases#21)
entries.root_cause: the contract supplied, as input, the very conclusion the check was supposed to reach -- a tautology oracle; and nothing proved the branch could still reach the conclusion once the label was removed
entries.gate_added: act-window now carries ordinary observations only (check time, actuation time, freeze-effective time, binding/source/generation); Q6 derives the binding loss itself
entries.evidence: harness selftest green with freeze_state absent from the observation set

entries.symptom: exit_code was produced before _apply_mutant() changed the final verdict, and the kill matrix then took observed[1:], discarding that first field -- leaving internally contradictory observations such as FAIL + EXECUTE + APPLY + target changed.
entries.found_by: ITU FG-TIDA round-3 review (use-cases#21)
entries.root_cause: no assertion crossed exit status against guard decision, attempted action and target state; the observation contract had never been shown to reject a contradictory record
entries.gate_added: exit status is recomputed from the final verdict, and _assert_observation_coherence() asserts agreement across the four fields
entries.evidence: a deliberately contradictory observation record now raises in the selftest

entries.symptom: The harness said mutations were applied after the runner had ruled, but M2-cache-read changed the input BEFORE the decision, and M1-M4 inject behavioural deviation around the implementation rather than mutating implementation.py; the description and the code described different layers.
entries.found_by: ITU FG-TIDA round-3 review (use-cases#21)
entries.root_cause: the README's mutant table had no 'class' column, so nothing connected the described layer to the implemented layer, and no gate parsed the description
entries.gate_added: the README mutant table gained a class column and check_readme_agreement() now validates it; gate 9 carries a MUTCLASS mutation against that column
entries.evidence: tampering the mutant class column now turns the selftest red

entries.symptom: On its first run, gate 9 found that 7 of the S5 selftest's 12 decision points had never been shown capable of failing: row-count truncation, target-vs-action, blinding, self-report ban, spec fields, row-4 trace, and surviving-mutant reporting all passed unconditionally.
entries.found_by: tools/checker-mutation.py, first run (this round)
entries.root_cause: the mutation suite guarded the artifact, not the guards; nothing in the repository asked of a check the question it asks of everyone else -- can it fail?
entries.gate_added: gate 9 with 7 new negative controls; every check now has a mutation that must be killed
entries.evidence: before: S9 FAILED, 7 findings; after: 12 checks killed, 7 controls load-bearing, 2 sentinels green

entries.symptom: AGENTS.md and index.md both described the gate list as 'seven gates' while .githooks/pre-commit ran nine; the count had drifted twice (8, then 9) with no gate noticing, because the number is restated as a literal in prose instead of read from the hook.
entries.found_by: this round, while adding rule 13/14 to AGENTS.md
entries.root_cause: the gate count had no single source of truth: it was asserted as a literal in several documents, and no gate compared those literals against the hook that actually defines the list
entries.gate_added: a gate-count consistency check in verify_release_consistency.py (any 'Runs all N gates' / 'the same N gates' literal in a living document must equal the hook's real count; CHANGELOG.md is excluded as a historical record) + the documents now point at the hook instead of restating a number
entries.evidence: with the check in place, restoring the literal 'seven gates' into AGENTS.md makes gate 6 fail, and restoring the hook-derived wording returns it to green -- the drift D-017 describes is now mechanically rejected

entries.symptom: gate-lint.py crashed with a bare KeyError: 'PARSE' when pointed at a file containing a syntax error: lint_source() emitted Finding('PARSE', ...) but RULES never registered 'PARSE', so every RULES[f.rid]['severity'] lookup raised instead of reporting the unparseable file.
entries.found_by: this round, running gate-lint against a tool that had a syntax error (defect-closure.py, mid-edit)
entries.root_cause: a finding's rule id was never required to resolve in RULES; nothing had ever fed gate-lint an unparseable file, so the crash path had no negative control and had never been shown to run
entries.gate_added: RULES['PARSE'] is now registered, and gate-lint --selftest feeds an unparseable source and asserts the PARSE finding appears with an id that resolves
entries.evidence: gate-lint --selftest now fires PARSE on an unparseable sample without crashing

entries.symptom: Entry D-017 was recorded as closed with a gate_added describing 'a gate-count consistency check in verify_release_consistency.py', but that check was not yet in the tree -- the ledger asserted a gate that did not exist, and gate 10 accepted the entry because it only validated that the field was a non-empty string.
entries.found_by: this round, cross-checking the ledger against the tree before adding more entries
entries.root_cause: gate 10 validated the SHAPE of gate_added but never its referent; a free-text claim of a gate is indistinguishable from a real one, so a premature closure passed. The ledger was acting as authority for a check that was not there.
entries.gate_added: defect-closure.py now extracts every path-like token from gate_added and requires it to resolve to an existing file, and any tools/*.py it names to be invoked by .githooks/pre-commit; two negative controls cover both branches (a missing gate, an unwired tool). Residual gap, stated rather than hidden: it can prove a named gate EXISTS and runs, not that the check inside it is the one described -- that stays a review-time judgement.
entries.evidence: the two new negative controls are caught by --selftest ('does not exist' and 'no gate hook invokes'), and the real ledger passes once D-017's check is actually present in verify_release_consistency.py

entries.symptom: Gate 12 (implementation mutation) scored killed 9 / 0.818 and failed on both CI matrix jobs (python 3.9 and python 3.12) at commit fc86dc5, while the same commit reported killed 11 / 1.000 on the developer machine. Two non-exempt mutants, NUM-001 ('0' -> '1') and CMP-001 ('==' -> '!='), were reported as surviving. They had not survived -- the child interpreter never executed them.
entries.found_by: our own gates workflow, run 37729789970, on the pushed commit fc86dc5 (both matrix jobs red at gate 12) -- the first time this gate had ever run in an environment where the interpreter's bytecode cache was enabled
entries.root_cause: Nothing asked the gate whether its runner was executing the artifact it had just written. CPython validates a .pyc against (source mtime truncated to whole seconds, source size); a same-size mutant written back to the same path inside the same second leaves both fields unchanged, so the child re-executed stale bytecode compiled from the unmutated source and the selftest passed. The defect was invisible on the machine that developed it only because that shell had PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE exported -- the remembered 'local 12/12 green' was itself an artifact of the environment, not a property of the tree.
entries.gate_added: tools/impl-mutation.py: the child runs with PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1, the scratch artifact is written with newline="", and a bytecode_cache_control deliberately reconstructs the stale-cache window and fails the gate when the runner reports that mutant as survived; tools/checker-mutation.py carries the same closure for the sibling tool.
entries.evidence: At the pre-fix revision, on one machine and one interpreter, removing PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE reproduces the CI reading exactly (killed 9, score 0.818, exit 1); restoring it returns killed 11 / 1.000. With the fix in place the same cache-enabled condition reports killed 11 / 1.000 and the bytecode-cache control stays quiet, and it fires when the cache is deliberately allowed back -- so the control is load-bearing rather than decorative.

entries.symptom: Seven files sat in the index with CRLF line endings and nothing in the toolchain objected. `.gitattributes` is `* -text`, so git performs no end-of-line conversion at all: the bytes are byte-exact on checkout, every manifest digest matches, and the run in which a CRLF was committed is indistinguishable from the run in which none was. The most consequential of the seven was `.githooks/pre-commit` itself -- a `#!/bin/sh` script the Linux shell (dash) refused with `set: Illegal option -`, so on the platform CI uses the gate list could not run at all. The commit that carried them, fc86dc5, was titled 'line-ending normalization' while its own tree still held seven CRLF blobs.
entries.found_by: this round, when the hook was copied into a Linux container to be re-run after CI failed at gate 12 -- the copy is what exposed the line endings
entries.root_cause: No gate looked at line endings anywhere. `-text` is required by the byte manifest (a converted checkout would produce different bytes on Windows and Linux, so every digest would differ by platform), but the same setting removes git's only automatic normalisation, so a CRLF is committed silently and every existing gate stays green. The property was asserted in a commit subject and enforced by nothing.
entries.gate_added: gate 13 runs tools/check-line-endings.py, which reads the INDEX blobs (git ls-files -s, then git cat-file blob) rather than the working tree, skips NUL-bearing blobs, prints path:line for each CRLF and exits non-zero on any hit; it is wired into .githooks/pre-commit and .github/workflows/gates.yml, and the six blobs still dirty at fc86dc5 were normalised to LF in the same pass.
entries.evidence: --selftest carries four controls and all four fire: a committed CRLF file is reported with a non-zero exit, a pure-LF repository passes silently, a CRLF hidden behind an LF working tree is still reported (the divergence control -- the shape a working-tree reader would miss), and a NUL-bearing blob is skipped. On this repository it prints 'OK: 70 file(s) in the index, no CRLF', because the seven blobs were normalised before the gate landed.

entries.symptom: The D-020 fix was copied into tools/checker-mutation.py on the strength of the class label alone, and the comment written with it asserted that this tool 'is exposed to the same window'. It is not. Measured on 2026-10-08: harness.py is executed as the __main__ script, so no harness bytecode file is produced for the file this gate rewrites; with the bytecode cache enabled a same-size mutant pinned to the same whole second is still killed, and removing the isolation by patch changes not one verdict (S9 stays green). A necessity that had never been measured was written down as fact -- in a repository whose rule 10 exists because of this exact mistake (D-010).
entries.found_by: this round, while trying to give the tool the self-probe dead control that had been authorised -- testing first whether such a control could fire, which is what showed the claim under it was false
entries.root_cause: The sibling sweep was run on the class label instead of the mechanism. 'Writes a file, then runs it through a child interpreter' matched, so the fix was copied; but masking also requires the rewritten file to be IMPORTED, because only imported modules get a bytecode cache -- a file run as __main__ is compiled fresh every time. Nothing in the repository requires a necessity claim to be measured, and an untested claim reads exactly like a tested one.
entries.gate_added: the comment in tools/checker-mutation.py now records the measurement instead of the assumption, and the isolation is kept and labelled belt-and-braces rather than presented as a closure. The proposed self-probe was deliberately withheld: the experiment above showed it could never fire, so it would have been a decorative control -- the very defect this ledger exists to record.
entries.evidence: Two readings on one machine and one interpreter. With the cache enabled the scratch package produces only the imported module's bytecode file and no harness one; a same-size mutant pinned to the same whole second exits 1 (killed) under both cache conditions; and the full gate returns exit 0 either way, including when its isolation is removed by patch (the run opened with 'baseline selftest (unmutated) -> PASS' and closed with 'S9 PASSED').

entries.symptom: One hook run printed, in the same screen, `─ gate 计数：✅ 活文档与真源一致（15 道）` directly above `═ 判定：❌ 不一致 ——` and its `❌ .github/workflows/gates.yml：声明 five gates，但真源 .githooks/pre-commit 有 15 道`. The section summary declared its section green while that section had just gone red. The failure itself was caught -- it entered the failure list, the verdict and the exit code -- so nothing was structurally lost, which is exactly why it went unnoticed: the run was red, the log was honest two lines below, and only the summary line lied. A reader who scans the section lines, or a log scraper keyed on a green tick, concludes the gate count is consistent.
entries.found_by: this round, while adding gates 14 and 15 -- the count check fired because a bare `five gates` had been written into the CI workflow's prose, and the summary line sitting above it stayed green. The two had never been seen together, because this check had never failed on this tree before.
entries.root_cause: The section summary was computed from `n_gates` -- is the canonical source readable -- instead of from the section's own failure list. `n_gates` is 15 for every tree that has a hook, so the green branch was taken on every input except a missing `.githooks/pre-commit`: the line could not go red for the failure it sat next to. The count check's findings were appended to the shared failure list correctly, which is why the verdict and the exit code disagreed with the summary rather than with the facts. Nothing required a section summary to be derived from its section's result, and nothing had ever shown this one able to fail -- which is the generalisable part: a status line that has never been seen red has not been shown to be capable of going red.
entries.gate_added: tools/verify_release_consistency.py now collects the count check's outcome in its own list and prints the section line from it -- red when the section failed, red when the canonical source is missing, green only otherwise. No new gate was added: the gate that already existed, invoked by both .githooks/pre-commit and .github/workflows/gates.yml, was repaired, so the repair reaches the same places every other gate does.
entries.evidence: Both states were read from the same line on a throwaway copy of the working tree. Pristine: `─ gate 计数：✅ 活文档与真源一致（15 道）`. With a bare `five gates` prepended to the CI workflow: `─ gate 计数：❌ 活文档与真源不一致（真源 15 道）` -- the summary now follows the verdict instead of contradicting it. The control driver lives at `_diag_ci_20261008/exp7_count_summary_contradiction.py` in the FG-TIDA working folder and asserts that the failing state's summary contains no green tick. The pre-fix contradiction was observed live in this round's hook output and is quoted verbatim in the symptom above.

entries.symptom: The gate added as 14/15 compares the hook's gate list against CI's, and its own docstring declared exactly one hole: a gate dropped from both lists. An independent review seat ran mutated copies of the repository and found that the hole was a family, not one shape. Three edits applied symmetrically to both lists all came back green: (a) the same gate dropped from both lists with the labels renumbered, (b) the same gate added to both lists, (c) the same gate's arguments changed on both sides. Only (a) was declared. And the compensating control the declaration named for it -- the N/M label discipline -- was measured rather than assumed: dropping the gate from both lists and renumbering stayed green, while dropping it and forgetting to renumber was caught. So the declared protection does not exist for an editor who follows the convention the labels exist to encourage, which is the careful path, not the careless one.
entries.found_by: the independent review seat for gate 14/15 on 2026-10-08, by mutating copies of the repository instead of reading the tool: thirteen mutated copies plus a positive control. Its own hand-written extractor found 15 gates on each side with gate 6 the only difference, matching the tool's own parse line for line -- so the finding is about the gate's scope, not about its parser.
entries.root_cause: Two causes with one shared origin. First, the declared scope was written from the shapes its author had imagined rather than from the shapes the mechanism cannot see, so the family was enumerated by imagination: deletion was declared, duplication and argument change were not. Second, the compensating control named in that declaration was never countersigned -- it was believed to cover the hole because it exists and had been seen to fire, not because it had been fed the exact input it is supposed to catch. That is the countersign test in the taxonomy's family D, applied to a promise rather than to a check.
entries.gate_added: check 4 in tools/check-gate-parity.py: neither list may run the same (script, arguments) pair twice. It needs no second registry, which is what the docstring had rejected as the cure, because a duplicate is a contradiction inside one list rather than a disagreement between two. Shown able to fail: the same pair was appended to both lists in the mutated copy and the gate returned exit 1 with 'runs tools/check-gate-parity.py [] twice (steps 15 and 16)', while the unmutated copy returned exit 0. Two controls were added to the gate's own self-test -- a red control appending the duplicate to both lists, and the pre-existing green control that runs tools/check-catalog.py twice with different arguments, which guards the new check against over-tightening into one that rejects a legitimate repeat. The known-limit section of tools/check-gate-parity.py now states all three shapes and carries the measurement that separates them, and no longer claims the label discipline covers what it does not. The two remaining shapes are left open and named, not papered over.
entries.evidence: Self-test: 11 controls pass with exit 0, up from 10, the added one being the duplicate control. On the 15-gate repository the gate prints 'OK: hook and CI agree on 15 gate(s), labels 1/15..15/15, 1 declared exception(s)' with exit 0. Replaying the review seat's mutated copies against the updated gate: the unmutated copy green, the symmetric-duplicate copy red, the symmetric-deletion copy green, the symmetric-argument copy green, the delete-without-renumber copy red -- so the newly closed shape changed verdict, and the two remaining holes stay exactly as the docstring now declares them. The full hook, all fifteen gates, prints 'pre-commit: all gates passed'.

entries.symptom: The Zenodo deposit workflow hard-coded the version string, the archive filename and the whole metadata document. The release that triggers it was therefore invisible to it: an archive named for a published tag would have carried metadata for a superseded one. Two further defects sat behind that one and were only reachable once the version was read from the tag. First, `actions/newversion` returns a draft that inherits the previous version's files, and the workflow uploaded the new archive without deleting the inherited one, so a correct-looking run would publish two archives. Second, the step that set the deposit metadata read its inputs from environment variables that the shell never exported, so it would have failed at runtime. And because the deposit path had no local gate at all, none of this was observable: the repository's own release-consistency gate checks the git tag, the manifest and the licence, and never looks at the Release, the deposit, or the version strings in the documents that describe them.
entries.found_by: An external question -- 'is the GitHub version 0.1.0, is everything consistent, and was it actually tested from an outsider's point of view' -- followed by an independent adversarial review seat that ran commands rather than reading the file. It compared the published Release list, the Zenodo record, and the version strings in llms.txt and docs/where-to-find-us.md against the canonical tag, and it found that the deposit step could not have failed locally because the version it would check against was written into the step itself.
entries.root_cause: The deposit machinery was treated as prose. A file that decides what an archive *is* had its identity written as a literal in three places, and nothing compared those literals to the tag that would invoke it. The rule this repository already has for that shape -- a value that describes the artifact is stated once -- had been applied to the gate count and nowhere else. Behind that: the deposit path was the only part of the release pipeline that could not be executed locally, so it had no way to be shown failing, and a component that cannot be shown failing drifts while every visible gate stays green.
entries.gate_added: The version, the archive name and the publication date are now derived from the tag under deposit (a workflow_dispatch input, or the Release's tag_name), and a ref that is not vX.Y.Z stops the run. The archive is checked for the version it claims before upload, and the published record is checked after. The draft's inherited files are listed and deleted, with each deletion's status checked, before the upload -- whose status is checked before the irreversible publish. The metadata step's inputs are exported, and a leftover draft is discarded through the API rather than through a shell variable. The run is idempotent: a version already published under the concept is a successful no-op. Shown able to fail: a local rehearsal drives the extracted step against a fake deposit API in five scenarios -- a correct run exits 0 with exactly one file published, while a rejected token, an inherited file that survives deletion, and a record that reports the wrong version each exit non-zero. The harness carries its own canary: if the fake API is never called it reports a harness defect, which is how the first version of the rehearsal was caught reaching the real network.
entries.evidence: Local: _verify_workflow.py -- 0 CRLF, YAML parses, all three embedded Python blocks compile, and the version guard accepts v0.1.2/0.1.2 and rejects main/v0.1. _rehearse_deposit.py -- five scenarios, VERDICT PASS (POS rc=0 publishing exactly sfc_v0.1.2.tar.gz; bad_token, keep_inherited and version_drift rc=1). Repository: manifest regenerated (73 files, set digest 501a3acb...), and bash .githooks/pre-commit prints 'pre-commit: all gates passed' across all sixteen gates. Sibling scan: git grep -lE '0.1.[0-9]' returns fourteen tracked files; the ones that are current claims rather than history -- README.md, INTEGRITY.md, CITATION.cff, .zenodo.json, llms.txt, docs/where-to-find-us.md -- are the face-level mirrors that still have no gate, and closing that half is tracked separately in the release-face audit pack.

entries.symptom: Six files each stated which version of this catalog is the canonical one -- README.md, INTEGRITY.md, .zenodo.json, CITATION.cff, llms.txt and docs/where-to-find-us.md -- and they did not agree with each other or with the git tag. The repository had a release-consistency gate and it was green: it compared the git tag, the manifest and the licence, and it never opened the GitHub Release, never opened the Zenodo record, and never read the version strings in the documents that describe the release. It also never checked that the branch-protection required status checks still name a job that exists, so a renamed job would leave a rule that waits for a report that can never arrive.
entries.found_by: An external question -- whether the published version and the in-tree version, and the version told by each document, are actually the same -- answered by running commands against the live repository rather than reading the files. `gh api .../releases` returned an empty list, `gh api .../branches/main/protection` returned only the two contexts the gate itself checked, and the Zenodo record under the concept DOI carried a version string that matched neither the tag nor the documents. The gate was green throughout, which is the defect: the evidence was produced locally and the claim was about the published face.
entries.root_cause: The release was treated as whatever the working tree said it was. Every gate this repository owns runs in a checkout of the repository, so a gate can only ever see the local copy of a version string; nothing compared that copy to the manifest of the release that a reader actually cites. The gap was not in the checks' logic but in their scope: a local gate cannot contradict a remote fact it never fetches, and the repository had no gate whose reach extended past the checkout. Behind that, the version was stated in eight places with no single source, so even a reader comparing two of them could not tell which one was authoritative.
entries.gate_added: A seventeenth gate, tools/verify_release_face.py, in two scopes. In-tree (runs on every commit, no network): it derives the one release version from the files that declare it, fails if two declarations disagree, and then asserts that every face -- the tag, the six documents, the archive line, the dates -- tells that same version and no other. Published (runs on a daily schedule and on every release, in .github/workflows/release-face-remote.yml with a token that can read repository administration): it asserts that the tag exists, that a GitHub Release exists for it, that the Zenodo record under the concept DOI is at that version, that the archived DOI cited in-tree is a record that exists, and that the branch-protection required checks name jobs the workflows actually declare. A face that cannot be reached is a failure, not a skip -- rule 12 is written into the gate -- with a single declared exception (R5, the required-check probe) that reports NOT VERIFIED and is counted rather than passed. No literal version remains in the gate: the GitHub side derives its tag from the tree and the archive side derives its version from the tag.
entries.evidence: Shown able to fail: tools/verify_release_face.py --selftest runs 24 cases and passes. Each face has its own counterexample -- a version that disagrees with the tag, two declarations that disagree with each other, a Release that does not exist, a Zenodo record set that lacks the declared version, a required check that no job reports, a renamed job that leaves a dead rule, an `on:` child key mistaken for a job, a published face that cannot be fetched, and a token without administration read. The suite also carries a canary: it fails if a case's fake API was never called, which is how an earlier version of the suite was caught passing without exercising the network path. On the real tree the in-tree scope reports the six faces aligned at 0.1.2, and the published scope run locally against the live repository reports R1/R2/R4 failing (no tag v0.1.2 yet, no Release, branch protection present) -- the state that the closing sequence in the audit pack is queued to change. Repository: manifest regenerated and bash .githooks/pre-commit green across all seventeen gates.

entries.symptom: The Zenodo deposit step of the release pipeline crashed on its first real run with `json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)`, after the token check had passed and the concept DOI and the latest published deposition had both been read successfully. The step decoded every HTTP response as JSON, and Zenodo answers DELETE with 204 and no body at all, so the step that clears the files a new draft inherits was the one that failed. The deposit never reached publish: a GitHub Release was published for v0.1.2 and no archive followed it, which is the exact shape this catalog exists to name.
entries.found_by: The release pipeline itself, not the offline rehearsal. Publishing the v0.1.2 GitHub Release triggered run 37913060210 of `Zenodo Deposit`; it failed after 18 seconds, and the log shows the traceback with the token, the concept DOI and the latest deposition all resolved. The rehearsal that was supposed to stand in for this run was green at the time, which is the defect rather than a detail of it. Recorded as `source: self-test` because this repository's own checking found it; note that the ledger's source enum has no value for 'found by running the release for real', and that gap is written here rather than flattened away.
entries.root_cause: The rehearsal's fidelity, not its coverage. The harness drove five scenarios and each one asserted the right thing, but the stand-in API was kinder than the API it stood in for: it answered DELETE with a JSON object while Zenodo answers 204 with no body. A fake more forgiving than the real thing cannot produce the failure the real thing produces, so no number of added scenarios would have caught this. The same mistake hid twice in one run: `keep_inherited` also passed for the wrong reason -- it crashed on the empty body rather than reaching the assertion it had been written to exercise, and a case that fails for an unintended reason is not a case.
entries.gate_added: Two changes, one on each side of the same boundary. (1) The step no longer decodes blindly: a `body_of()` helper returns None for an empty body and the raw text for a body that is not JSON, and every consumer now refuses with a sentence instead of a traceback -- the deposition list, the new version's links, the new draft and the publish response are each checked for the type they must have. (2) The fixture is now faithful: the fake answers DELETE with 204 and an empty body, a `delete_body` field records what was served so a later edit cannot soften it again, and a sixth scenario (`notjson`) asserts that a 200 whose body is HTML ends in a sentence rather than a traceback. The harness maps an uncaught exception to 99, so the case requires rc=1 -- a clean refusal. The same tightening was applied to the pre-existing cases: `keep_inherited` and `version_drift` must now fail with rc=1 rather than merely somewhere non-zero.
entries.evidence: Shown able to fail, in the right direction, before it was believed. With the fixture corrected and the workflow untouched, the rehearsal reproduced the production failure exactly -- POS rc=99 with the same JSONDecodeError at the same line, `notjson` rc=99, and `keep_inherited` passing on a crash rather than on its own assertion. Only then was the step changed. Afterwards the same six scenarios report POS rc=0 publishing exactly `sfc_v0.1.2.tar.gz`; bad_token, keep_inherited, version_drift and notjson rc=1; already rc=0 with nothing uploaded. The two gate files that also decode external JSON, tools/verify_release_face.py and tools/verify_release_consistency.py, were scanned for the same shape and both already wrap their decode in try/except, so the workflow was the only instance. Manifest regenerated; bash .githooks/pre-commit green across all seventeen gates.

entries.symptom: The Zenodo deposit step refused to deposit, reporting `no published deposition under concept 23051637 to version from`, while record 10.5281/zenodo.23051638 was published and publicly visible under that exact concept. It had read that same deposition successfully on its previous run. The only thing that had changed in between was the step's own discard of a leftover draft.
entries.found_by: Run 37915051489 of `Zenodo Deposit`, the run after a crash. Its log reads `concept DOI id: 23051637`, then `discarded leftover draft 23259866 (HTTP 204)`, then the error. Run 37913060210, the run before it, reads `latest published deposition: 23051638` at the same point, which is what made two consecutive runs of the same code disagree in public instead of looking plausible.
entries.root_cause: The step reasoned from a snapshot taken before the change it had just made. Zenodo's deposit API answers `GET /depositions` with the draft alone while a draft is open under a concept: the published versions are not in that response at all. So the listing the step had already fetched was the one listing in which the answer to its own question could not appear, and after discarding the draft it kept using it. Confirmed by the third run: with the leftover draft gone, the unchanged code path saw `latest published deposition: 23051638` again and deposited normally. A second defect was latent in the same ordering -- the idempotency check also ran before the discard, so a version that was already deposited would have looked absent and had a duplicate record minted for it.
entries.gate_added: (1) The step clears leftover drafts first and re-reads the deposition list afterwards, refusing with a sentence if that read fails or finds nothing. (2) The idempotency check moved after the re-read, for the same reason. (3) The rehearsal's fake now models the API instead of flattering it: every scenario starts with a leftover draft open, the published record is not listed until the draft is discarded, `discard` answers 204 with an empty body (and `discard_body` is asserted, so a later edit cannot soften it), and `listings >= 2` is required for the scenarios that must discard one -- a step that never re-reads the list cannot pass. The behaviour and both run ids are written into the workflow's own header, because the next person to reorder those two statements will not read this ledger.
entries.evidence: The mutation is the evidence. With the fixture corrected and the re-read removed from a throwaway copy of the workflow, the rehearsal reproduces production exactly: POS rc=1, calls=2, listings=1, FAIL -- one listing, taken before its own discard, with the published version missing from it, which is run 37915051489 in miniature. With the re-read restored, the same six scenarios report POS rc=0 listings=2 publishing exactly `sfc_v0.1.2.tar.gz`; already rc=0 listings=2 with nothing uploaded; bad_token, keep_inherited, version_drift and notjson rc=1. Production closes the loop: run 37915513109, after run 2 had discarded the draft, reads `latest published deposition: 23051638` and deposits version 0.1.2 as 10.5281/zenodo.23260442.

entries.symptom: The strict published-face run failed with `R3 Zenodo record FAIL -- Zenodo API unreachable from here (HTTP Error 400: BAD REQUEST)` and `verdict: FAIL -- 1 finding(s), 1 not verified`, against an API that was answering in milliseconds. The reader is sent to look at the network; the problem was the request.
entries.found_by: Run 37913060225 of `release-face-remote`, logged by the release that triggered it. The 400 was then read through a channel that does not go through this repository at all, which is the only reason the real cause could be quoted rather than guessed: {"status": 400, "message": "A validation error occurred.", "errors": [{"field": "size", "messages": ["Page size cannot be greater than 25. Please use authenticated requests to increase the limit to 100."]}]}
entries.root_cause: Two wrong assumptions in one probe, and a blanket `except` over both. The probe asked the public records API for `size=100`, which that API refuses for an unauthenticated caller -- the cap is 25 -- and it queried the concept by DOI string in a field the index does not key on. Either would have produced a rejection, and `except Exception` turned every rejection into the same sentence: unreachable. A gate that fails for the wrong cause is worse than one that passes: it spends the reader's attention and leaves the defect it was written to catch exactly where it was.
entries.gate_added: (1) The probe walks pages at the size an unauthenticated caller is allowed (`size=25`, following the API's own `links.next`) instead of asking for a page it may not have, and names the field the index keys on (`conceptrecid`). (2) `urllib.error.HTTPError` is caught separately from a transport failure and reported as a refusal carrying its own status code and body, so 'the API said no' can no longer be printed as 'the API was not there'. (3) The network edge moved into `RealAPI._open`, so the selftest drives the real implementation through a rejection and across a paginated concept instead of through a stub that returns a canned tuple. (4) `run_case` gained `want_fail_text` and `forbid_fail_text`: a case can now pin the *reason*, because a right failure with a wrong cause is what no `want_fail=True` can see.
entries.evidence: Two new cases and a mutation for each. `R3-api-refused` feeds the probe the 400 verbatim and requires the failure to name the refusal and to not contain the word 'unreachable'; `R3-paginated` puts the record carrying the release version on page 2 of 26, requires the walk to reach it, and carries a canary asserting the second page was actually fetched. Restoring the old sentence ('unreachable' in place of 'refused the request (HTTP 400)') turns `R3-api-refused` red, on that case and no other. Removing the follow-next-page step turns `R3-paginated` red. The corrected query was confirmed against the live API before it was written down: `q=conceptrecid:23051637&allversions=true&size=25` returns both versions of the concept (hits.total = 2, one of them version 0.1.2).

entries.symptom: Once version 0.1.2 had been deposited as 10.5281/zenodo.23260442, the README's DOI badge and its archived sentence -- and INTEGRITY.md's archived line -- still pointed at 10.5281/zenodo.23051638, the 0.1.0 record. A reader following the repository's own citation pointer landed on the superseded archive, and face R3 of tools/verify_release_face.py reported PASS.
entries.found_by: The in-tree run of gate 17, after the deposit landed: it printed `archived DOI / version 10.5281/zenodo.23051638 @ 0.1.0` beside `verdict: PASS`, which is the two lines that cannot both be right once 0.1.2 exists. The README carried a forward-looking sentence written before the deposit -- 'until it lands, the newest archived version is the 0.1.0 record' -- and nothing turned it into work when it landed.
entries.root_cause: The archive-line check asked a smaller question than it was credited with answering. It compared the sentence against the record the sentence itself names, so any internally consistent line passed, and it checked separately that *some* record under the concept carries the release version. 'A record carrying the release version exists' and 'the repository points readers at it' are two different claims, and only the first was checked -- so the countersign test fails: fed the exact thing it exists to catch (an archive line naming the previous record while the concept already holds the released one), it stayed green. INTEGRITY.md had in fact written the missing half down in prose -- 'the lag cannot become permanent without something going red' -- and that promise had no mechanism behind it.
entries.gate_added: R3 gained the half its own documentation claimed: when a published record under the concept carries the release version, the in-tree archive line must name that record, and the failure says which DOIs are involved. The lag is still allowed while a release is in flight, which is why the new assertion fires only once such a record exists. The six faces were then moved to 0.1.2 -- README's badge and archived sentence, INTEGRITY.md's archival note, and the paragraph that promised the red now describes what actually enforces it.
entries.evidence: `R3-archive-superseded` is the countersign: a tree whose archive line names the previous record while the released one is published beside it under the same concept, asserted to fail with the words 'superseded archive' -- so the case pins the reason, not merely the failure. The fixture the selftest builds as good (`GOOD`) was itself corrected, because it had been constructed in the same stale shape: its archived line named the 9.9.8 record while its release was 9.9.9. In the live tree, gate 17 now reports `archived DOI / version 10.5281/zenodo.23260442 @ 0.1.2` and passes.

entries.symptom: When the selftest's canary fired -- the fake API was called fewer times than a case required -- the run died with `TypeError: %d format: a real number is required, not str` from inside the canary's own error message, and the selftest exited without printing a single case result. The condition the canary exists to report was reported as a formatting crash in the reporter.
entries.found_by: A mutation, not a scenario. Removing the follow-next-page step from a throwaway copy of tools/verify_release_face.py made `R3-paginated` fail its canary for the first time in the file's life -- and the first failure of a check is the first execution of its failure path.
entries.root_cause: The canary's failure branch had never run, so nobody had ever read it: `"the fake API was called %d time(s), expected >= %d" % (k, got, want)` feeds the dict key (`"zen"`) to the first `%d`. Every prior case either satisfied its canary or failed earlier for another reason, which is exactly the state a check is in when it has not been shown capable of failing. The consequence was not a silent pass but something nearly as bad: the case's real diagnosis was replaced by a traceback pointing at the reporter, so the reader is told to fix the wrong file.
entries.gate_added: The message is repaired and names the counter it is about. More to the point, the defect was found by mutation rather than by a scenario, and the mutation that found it is now the reason the branch exists: `R3-paginated` is the first case in the suite whose canary can fail, and the k mutation that removes the pagination walk is what drives it.
entries.evidence: Before: the pagination mutation produced `TypeError: %d format: a real number is required, not str` with no case lines, and the mutation harness could not tell a caught mutation from a crashed run. After: the same mutation reports `R3-paginated` as the failing case, by name, which is what makes the pagination walk a load-bearing step rather than a decoration.

entries.symptom: The strict published-face run printed `R3   Zenodo record   FAIL   no record under the concept` and `verdict: FAIL -- 1 finding(s)`, against a concept under which Zenodo's own records API returns two published records. The gate did not stay silent -- it fired and named a cause that was false. A reader acts on 'there is nothing deposited' by depositing again; there was nothing to deposit.
entries.found_by: the scheduled release-face-remote.yml run 37958934049, surfaced by an outside-in verification pass on 2026-10-10 that resolved the concept DOI against the records API directly instead of trusting the gate's sentence
entries.root_cause: `((data or {}).get('hits') or {}).get('hits') or []` in `zenodo_records()` gave one value -- the empty list -- to two different situations: 'the concept holds nothing' and 'this body is not the search envelope this code knows how to read'. A transport that answers 200 with a shape the code cannot parse therefore arrives at the caller as an empty result, and the caller had a sentence ready for an empty result. That is SF-004 (`or []` as a sentinel for failure) wearing the face of SF-012 (the check fails and blames the wrong cause). It is the second escape of the class D-029 closed the same day: D-029 fixed the shape it had been shown -- an HTTP refusal, and a body that is not JSON -- and the case set it added (`R3-api-refused`, `R3-paginated`) never contained a 200 whose body *parses* but is not the envelope. The instance was closed; the class was not.
entries.gate_added: (1) `tools/verify_release_face.py` `zenodo_records()` now requires `hits` to be an object carrying `total` before any record is counted, and otherwise returns an unreadable-page refusal that names the top-level keys it did receive, so 'nothing is there' and 'this page cannot be read' are two findings with two sentences. (2) Two cases in the selftest: `R3-envelope-shape`, a negative control feeding a 200 body that is not the envelope and requiring the failure to name the shape and to not contain the string 'no record under the concept'; and `R3-genuinely-empty`, its positive counterpart, which requires a well-formed envelope holding nothing to still be named an empty concept so the shape check cannot pass by never calling a concept empty. (3) The `R3-paginated` fixture now carries the envelope's `total`, because the fixture, not the API, was the thing that omitted it.
entries.evidence: On the unmodified file the new case produced `R3: Zenodo holds no record at all under concept 10.5281/zenodo.11111110` -- a definite finding manufactured from an unreadable page, reproducing the remote run. With the change, the same input yields `Zenodo answered HTTP 200 but not with a records envelope (top-level keys: message, status)`, the fabricated sentence is absent (`forbid_fail_text`), and the suite is 30/30 where it was 28/28 before. The in-tree scope (`--no-remote`) still prints `verdict: PASS -- every face tells the same story`, and `tools/make-manifest.py --check` reported `modified: tools/verify_release_face.py` before regeneration, so the content manifest is a gate that fires rather than a decoration.

entries.symptom: The scheduled run after D-032 was fixed reported `R3 Zenodo record FAIL Zenodo refused the request (HTTP 504): <html>504 Gateway Time-out</html>` and `verdict: FAIL -- 1 finding(s)`. The cause named was now true -- that was the point of D-032 -- but the consequence was still wrong: a momentary gateway timeout was published in the same channel as repository drift, so a daily gate goes red for an event that says nothing about this repository, and the reader is asked to investigate a deposit that is fine.
entries.found_by: the scheduled release-face-remote.yml run 37965255375, triggered as the re-verification of the D-032 fix, read against the question 'is this red about us or about them?'
entries.root_cause: `zenodo_records()` treated every transport answer as final. For a 4xx that is correct -- a rejection is the answer. For a 5xx it is not: 429/500/502/503/504 say 'ask again', and asking once converted an upstream hiccup into a repository finding. The retry is the standard remedy and its absence was the defect: without it, 'cannot verify right now' and 'verified false' leave this function as the same tuple, which is the same conflation D-032 fixed one layer down.
entries.gate_added: `tools/verify_release_face.py` retries the retryable statuses (429/500/502/503/504) up to `ZENODO_ATTEMPTS = 3` with linear backoff via `_sleep()` (split out so a case drives the timing without waiting), and still returns a finding when the attempts run out -- now carrying `after N attempts` so a flake is distinguishable from a wall. Two cases: `R3-retry-recovers` (a 504 then a good page must be decided by the second answer, not the first) and `R3-retry-exhausted` (three 504s must still fail, and the finding must name the attempt count). Both were added and run *before* the retry existed: `selftest FAILED: 2 of 32` with `fails=1 (want 0)` and `the failure does not name 'refused the request (HTTP 504) after 3 attempts'`.
entries.evidence: Before: `selftest FAILED: 2 of 32 case(s)` and both new case ids printed as `x`. After: `selftest PASSED: 32 cases`, exit 0, and the two productions paths are pinned -- `R3-api-refused` still expects exactly one call for a 400 (a refusal is not retried) while `R3-retry-exhausted` expects three for a 504 block. The real run that motivated it: https://github.com/zhaoxinghua09-cell/silent-failure-catalog/actions/runs/37965255375
